rule: Smooth motion requires gradual and consistent angle changes between frames. Sudden large increments violate physical continuity.
In physically valid sequences, the angular velocity between consecutive frames should remain approximately constant.
A sudden angle jump greater than 50 degrees between two consecutive frames indicates an unrealistic discontinuity in rotation.
Real-world rigid body rotation follows smooth trajectories. Abrupt angle changes beyond physical limits are signs of generated or synthetic artifacts.
A physically valid transformation preserves the geometric identity of the object. Circles must remain circles; squares must remain squares throughout the sequence.
Shape morphing mid-sequence violates geometric rigidity. The contour count and structure should remain stable across all frames.
Distortion of a shape, such as a square becoming rectangle-like or a triangle becoming skewed, signals a physically inconsistent transformation.
Frames in a valid sequence must form a continuous temporal chain with no missing or corrupted intermediate states.
Frame discontinuity, where one or more frames appear as noise or completely different content, is a hallmark of AI-generated motion errors.
Uniform rotational motion maintains a constant angular increment. High variance in frame-to-frame angle differences indicates non-uniform and potentially invalid motion.
In the absence of external torque, a rotating rigid body maintains constant angular velocity. Irregular speed changes break this physical law.
Without an applied force, a rotating object cannot spontaneously reverse its direction of rotation. Multiple direction reversals in a sequence indicate physical impossibility.
Axis change in rotation — where the rotation direction reverses unexpectedly — violates Newton's first law of motion and marks the sequence as invalid.
A complete motion sequence must contain all expected frames. Missing frames reduce temporal resolution and make motion analysis unreliable.
High angular acceleration between frames without a physical cause is a sign of synthetic generation error. Natural motion follows smooth acceleration profiles.
Jerk — the rate of change of acceleration — should be minimal in physically plausible rigid body motion. Excessive jerk signals an invalid sequence.
A physically valid transformation sequence satisfies: shape preservation, smooth rotation, constant angular velocity, and temporal continuity.
Generative AI systems often produce visually plausible but physically inconsistent motion. Rule-based validation catches these violations that perceptual models miss.
